data.text/html:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo, explained by touching it

Picture a walker in complete darkness exploring a mountain range, step by step, where each footstep depends only on where they stand right now. Somehow, the walker ends up mapping the whole landscape. This notebook follows the video (DataMListic) chapter by chapter: accept-reject sampling → Markov chains → Monte Carlo → the stationary distribution → MCMC in action → burn-in → detailed balance. Color language (same as the video): ■ green = accepted / kept samples, ■ red = rejected samples or burn-in, ■ gold = the target distribution / true value, ■ blue = independent samples or proposals.

data.text/markdown:
1 · Why not just throw darts? (accept-reject sampling)

The naive way to sample from a weird density ||(p(x)||): draw a bounding box around it, throw points uniformly inside, keep the ones under the curve (green), throw away the ones above (red). ||[\text{acceptance rate} = \frac{\text{area under } p(x)}{\text{area of the box}}||]It works, but in the video "out of 30 samples, we're rejecting most of them." And the box gets relatively huge as dimensions grow. Press ▶ throw below.

The curse of dimensionality

Even for the friendliest target, a ball inside its bounding cube, the acceptance rate is ||(\dfrac{\text{vol(ball)}}{\text{vol(cube)}} = \dfrac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)\,2^d}||), which collapses as dimension ||(d||) grows. This is the video's "acceptance rates that drop to less than 1%".

data.text/markdown:
2 · Key insight: let each sample remember where we just were

Independent sampling (blue) throws away everything it learned. A Markov chain creates dependence instead: ||[x_{n+1} \sim T(\,\cdot \mid x_n)||]The next state depends only on the present, not the past (Andrey Markov's memoryless property). In the video, a yellow particle hops around a circular network of states, deciding where to go based only on its current position. Below is that ring. Each state ||(i||) stays put, steps clockwise, or steps counter-clockwise. You control how much it prefers clockwise moves. Watch where the particle spends its time.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Monte Carlo: estimate by averaging random samples

"Imagine trying to find the average of this distribution. Analytically, we need complex integrals." Monte Carlo swaps the integral for an average: ||[\mathbb{E}[x] = \int x\,p(x)\,dx \;\approx\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} x_n, \qquad x_n \sim p||]Our two-peak target has true mean ||(0.3\cdot(-2) + 0.7\cdot 2 = 0.8||) (gold line). The running average (red) of the green samples converges to it, with error shrinking like ||(1/\sqrt{N}||).

The rest of the lesson is about what to do when you \u003cstrong\u003ecan't\u003c/strong\u003e, and that's where Markov chains come in.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · The stationary-distribution trick

Section 2 showed that a Markov chain run long enough spends a fixed fraction of time in each state, its stationary distribution π. MCMC engineers the transition rule so that π equals the target p. "No matter where we started, the red, blue, or green chains all converge to spending time proportional to the height of our target. After enough steps, 30% of samples are in this peak, 70% in that peak." Below, three chains start at very different places. Track the fraction of time each spends in the right peak (x > 0).

data.text/markdown:
5 · MCMC in action: the Metropolis walker

The algorithm the video animates (random-walk Metropolis):
  1. From the current point ||(x||), propose ||(y = x + \varepsilon||), with ||(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, s^2)||) (blue dot)
  2. Accept with probability ||(\alpha = \min\!\left(1, \dfrac{p(y)}{p(x)}\right)||) and move there (green), otherwise reject and stay put (red flash; ||(x||) is recorded again)
Uphill moves are always accepted. Downhill moves are accepted sometimes, which keeps the walker from getting stuck on one summit. Only the ratio ||(p(y)/p(x)||) is needed, so the normalizing constant never matters. That's why MCMC works for Bayesian posteriors.

7 · Why it works: detailed balance

"For any two states X and Y, the flow of probability from X to Y, ||(P(X)\,T(Y\mid X)||), must exactly equal the flow from Y back to X, ||(P(Y)\,T(X\mid Y)||)." ||[\underbrace{p(x)\,T(y\mid x)}_{\text{flow } x\to y} \;=\; \underbrace{p(y)\,T(x\mid y)}_{\text{flow } y\to x}\quad\text{for all } x,y \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; p \text{ is stationary.}||](Sum both sides over ||(x||): ||(\sum_x p(x)T(y\mid x) = p(y)||).) Metropolis gets this for free: with a symmetric proposal, ||(p(x)\min\!\big(1,\tfrac{p(y)}{p(x)}\big) = \min(p(x),p(y))||), which is symmetric in ||(x,y||). Below is a 6-state ring. Set the target weights, pick an acceptance rule, and check the flows.
